To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the hind limb flexor withdrawal reflex is suppressed by electrical midbrain stimulation and that reflex suppression is mediated by parametrically distinct, but pharmacologically similar, mechanisms in the periaqueductral gray and lateral reticular formation.

the hind limb flexor withdrawal reflex in the anesthetized rat is under parametric and pharmacological control from the midbrain periventricular and periaqueduct gray (PVG and PAG, respectively) and lateral reticular formation, and the PVG and PAG exert parametric control, while the lateral reticular formation exerts parametric and pharmacologic control over the reflex.
the flexion withdrawal reflex to a noxious stimulus applied to the hind paw is suppressed parametrically and pharmacologically by electrical stimulation of the midbrain PAG and LRF in rats.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of the neural control of the flexion reflex.
the study of pain mechanisms in the spinal cord and brain.
the neuroanatomical and neurochemical basis of pain modulation in the spinal cord.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the midbrain PAG and LRF exert parametrically and pharmacologically distinct inhibitions of nociceptive flexor responses.
PAG and LRF have a parametrically but different pharmacological control on the flexion reflex.

PAG stimulation reduces the magnitude and temperature‐response slope of the flexion withdrawal reflex, while LRF stimulation reduces the temperature‐response slope and shifts it toward higher temperatures.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the hind limb flexor reflex is under parametrized but not pharmacologically different control by midbrain structures.
the flexion withdrawal reflex is under parametrizable but pharmacologically distinct midbrain inhibitory controls, and that these controls are mediated by serotoninergic and cholinergic neurons.
the flexion withdrawal reflex is under parametic and pharmacological distinct controls in the midbrain.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the flexion withdrawal reflex is under parametrable, but not pharmacologically, distinct midbrain inhibitory controls.

the PAG and the LRF are involved in the control of the flexion reflex, but the PAG appears to be more involved in the control the flexion reflex threshold and the LRF appears to be more directly involved in the control in the reflex magnitude.
the flexion response is under parametric control in the midbrain.
